blocks.text: *Bayram* means a holiday or festival, and twice a year Turkey has a long one, when millions of people travel to spend a few days with their families. These two bayrams are the great holidays of Islam, and in Turkey they are also the great family occasions of the year.

**Ramazan Bayramı** marks the end of Ramadan (*Ramazan*), the month of fasting, and lasts three days. It is also widely known as **Şeker Bayramı**, the sugar holiday, and sweets are offered to every visitor. **Kurban Bayramı**, the festival of the sacrifice, lasts four days and recalls the story of İbrahim (Abraham), who was ready to sacrifice his son. Families who can afford it have a sheep, goat or cow slaughtered; the meat is traditionally divided into three parts and shared with relatives, neighbours and people in need.

Both follow the Islamic calendar, whose months follow the moon. Its year is about eleven days shorter than the solar year, so each bayram comes about eleven days earlier every year and moves slowly through the seasons. In 2026, Ramazan Bayramı began on 20 March and Kurban Bayramı on 27 May. The day before a bayram is the *arife*, and its afternoon is already a public holiday.

On the first morning people put on new clothes, the *bayramlık*, and the visits begin, usually with the oldest members of the family. Younger people greet their elders by kissing their right hand and touching it to their forehead, a gesture of respect called *el öpmek*. Children who do so get sweets, chocolates or a little money, the *bayram harçlığı*, and in many neighbourhoods they go from door to door collecting them. Hosts offer *lokum* (Turkish delight), baklava and coffee. Many families also visit the graves of their relatives during the holiday.
The usual greetings are *İyi bayramlar!* (Happy holidays!) and *Bayramınız kutlu olsun!* (May your bayram be blessed!).

blocks.title: Kızım, oğlum
blocks.text: Older people often call any girl or young woman *kızım* (my daughter) and any boy or young man *oğlum* (my son). It is a warm way of speaking, not a sign that they are related.
Here is a bayram visit in the Turkish of this unit:

lines.tr: Sağ ol, kızım. Sana da iyi bayramlar!
lines.en: Thank you, dear. Happy holidays to you too!
My older brother and sister are coming too.

lines.tr: Çok güzel! Şekerimiz de var, çikolatamız da.
lines.en: Lovely! We have sweets, and chocolate too.

questions.q: Why does a bayram fall on a different date every year?
options: The government picks a new date each year
questions.explain: The Islamic year is about eleven days shorter than the solar year.

questions.q: How do children usually greet their elders at bayram?
questions.explain: *El öpmek*: they kiss the right hand and touch it to their forehead.

questions.q: In the dialogue, what does *ağabeyim ve ablam* mean?
options: my older brother and my older sister
